abstract: Summary Tubo-ovarian high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC), the most lethal gynecologic malignancy, initially responds to platinum-based chemotherapy, but due to frequent defects in the DNA damage response (DDR), most tumors develop resistance. The molecular mechanisms underlying clinical platinum resistance remain poorly defined with no biomarkers or targeted therapies to improve outcomes. Here, applying mass cytometry, we quantify phosphorylation and abundance of DDR proteins in carboplatin-treated HGSC cell line models. Despite similar levels of intranuclear platinum, a proxy for carboplatin uptake, cells follow divergent fates, reflecting DDR heterogeneity. Unsupervised analysis reveals a continuum of DDR states, and matrix factorization identifies eight protein modules. The activity of one module, containing canonical DDR proteins, increases in carboplatin-sensitive cells. Resistant cells engage a broader DDR protein module. These findings demonstrate the ability of single-cell proteomics to identify functional DDR states and reveal a DDR sensitivity module as a promising biomarker for clinical stratification and therapeutic decisions in HGSC.

Experimental model and subject details
Clinical data and tissue samples from patients were collected on the prospective Cambridge Translational Cancer Research Ovarian Study 04 (CTCR-OV04) with Research Ethics Committee approval 08/H0306/61. Patients provided written, informed consent for participation in this study and for the use of their donated tissue for the laboratory studies carried out in this work. Out of 93 samples three spontaneously immortalized continuous HGSOC cell lines were generated, named CIOV1, CIOV2, and CIOV3, and used as part of this study.
38
Cell lines
HeLa and OVCAR3 (American Type Culture Collection (ATCC)) and TYK-nu (National Institute of Biomedical Innovation, Japanese Collection of Research Bioresources Cell Bank (JCRB)) cell lines were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) (Gibco), McCoy’s 5A modified medium (Gibco) and Eagle’s minimal essential medium (EMEM) (ATCC) respectively supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Hyclone), 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin (Gibco) and 2 mM L-glutamine (Gibco). UWB1.289 and UWB1.289+BRCA1 cell lines (ATCC) (referred to in the main manuscript as BRCA1-and BRCA1+) were cultured in 50% RPMI-1640 (Gibco) supplemented with 2 mM L-glutamine, 25 mM sodium bicarbonate and 50% mammary epithelial growth medium (MEGM) (Lonza) supplemented with 3% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS). G-418 (200 mg/mL Geneticin from Gibco) was added to the media for the UWB1.289 BRCA+ cell line. JHOS2 (RIKEN BRC Cell Bank) cell line was cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium/Nutrient Mixture F-12 (DMEM/F-12 (Ham), Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS, 0.1 mM MEM non-essential amino acids (NEAA, Gibco) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin. CIOV1, CIOV2 and CIOV3 cell lines (Brenton Lab, University of Cambridge, UK) were cultured in DMEM/F-12 medium (Gibco) with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin. Cells were split every 2–3 days and kept in a humidified cell culture incubator at 37°C with an atmosphere of 95% air and 5% CO

Method details
Research design summary
To investigate tumor cell-intrinsic DDR mechanisms underlying carboplatin resistance and sensitivity, we performed single-cell mass cytometry (CyTOF) profiling across a panel of HGSC cell lines, that phenocopy human tumors, comprised of TYK-nu, the highly resistant UWB1.289 BRCA1-and UWB1.289 BRCA1+ isogenic pair, JHOS2, OVCAR3, and patient-derived models (CIOV1, CIOV2 and CIOV3). The UWB1.289 BRCA1-deficient cell line was derived from an HGSC tumor that recurred following primary debulking surgery and multiple lines of chemotherapy, including carboplatin/paclitaxel, paclitaxel alone, topotecan, and gemcitabine combined with doxorubicin. It harbors a clinically deleterious allele of
BRCA1
with loss of heterozygosity at the
BRCA1
locus rendering it null for BRCA1 protein function. The UWB1.289+BRCA1 cell line has partial restoration of BRCA1 function from stable expression of a
BRCA1
cDNA construct.
41
Cells were treated with carboplatin alone or in combination with other agents and sampled over time up to 96 h to capture dynamic DDR signaling. The CyTOF antibody panel quantified total and phosphorylated DDR proteins at single-cell resolution. Data were analyzed using unsupervised clustering and dimensionality reduction techniques to identify DDR modules and signaling trajectories across models with varying carboplatin sensitivity (
Figure 3
).

Antibodies used for CyTOF
All antibodies used for CyTOF were conjugated in-house (
Table S1
). Antibodies in carrier-free PBS were conjugated to metal-chelated polymers using the MaxPAR antibody conjugation kit (Standard BioTools) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Bismuth-chelated polymer labeling was performed using an in-house protocol.
85
Metal-labeled antibodies were diluted to 0.2–0.4 mg/mL in antibody stabilization solution (CANDOR Biosciences) and stored at 4°C. Each antibody was titrated to determine optimal working concentrations using positive and negative controls to ensure specificity and signal-to-noise performance. Additionally, the CIOV cell lines were characterized using our previously established HGSC tumor CyTOF antibody panel.
40
Final antibody concentrations were selected chosen were based on titration results yielding the optimal signal-to-noise ratio.
Sample processing and antibody staining for CyTOF
Frozen, fixed single-cell suspensions were thawed at room temperature (RT). For each sample, 1 × 10
6

After barcoding, cells were pooled, washed, and incubated for 5 min at RT with FcX block (Biolegend) to reduce non-specific antibody binding. Cells were then stained with the CyTOF antibody panel, washed, and incubated with the
191/193

Protocol for isolating nuclei
TYK-nu cells (4–5 × 10
6
) were harvested at 24 h, 48 h, 72 h, and 96 h following carboplatin treatment. Two untreated controls were harvested at 24 h and 96 h. Each sample was divided in half for processing by flow cytometry, and CyTOF analysis. For nuclear isolation, cell pellets were resuspended in 300 μL of cold lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 10 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl
2
, and 0.025% Igepal CA-630 in PBS) and incubated on ice for 10 min. The lysis reaction was quenched by adding 1.2 mL of cold CSM, followed by two washes with cold CSM (500 × g, 10 min, 4°C). The nuclei suspension was then filtered through a 35 μm cell strainer to remove debris and nuclear aggregates. Nuclei were then fixed in 1 mL of 1.6% PFA in PBS for 10 min at RT, washed twice with cold CSM, resuspended in 150–200 μL of CSM, snap-frozen on dry ice, and stored at −80°C until flow cytometry or CyTOF analysis. Nuclear purity was validated by three independent methods.
Processing isolated nuclei for flow cytometry
Fixed frozen TYK-nu cells or nuclei were thawed at RT and transferred to FACS tubes containing 1 mL of ice-cold CSM. Samples were centrifuged at 500 × g for 10 min at 4°C. Cells and nuclei were then stained with DAPI (500 μL, 0.1 μg/mL in PBS) for 10 min at RT to assess viability and nuclear content. Following staining, 1.5 mL of cold CSM was added, and samples were centrifuged again (500 × g, 10 min, 4°C). After two additional washes with ice-cold CSM, cells and nuclei were resuspended in cold CSM at a concentration of 1–2 × 10
6
cells/mL and 0.5–1 × 10
6
nuclei/mL, for introduction into the FACS LSRII. We used forward scatter (FSC) and side scatter (SSC) parameters to distinguish nuclei from whole cells (
Figure S8
A).
Processing isolated nuclei for immunofluorescence microscopy
Fixed frozen TYK-nu nuclei were thawed at RT, transferred to FACS tubes containing 1 mL of cold CSM and washed (500 × g, 10 min, 4°C). Samples were permeabilized in 100% ice-cold methanol (1 mL) for 20 min at 4°C, washed twice with cold CSM and stained with vimentin-A647 antibody (5 μL in 100 μL of reaction) (clone D21H3 from CST) for 30 min on ice. After the addition of 2 mL CSM, samples were washed twice with CSM followed by staining with DAPI (blue fluorescence channel) (1 μg/mL in CSM, 500 μL) for 10 min at room temperature. After two washes with CSM, nuclei were resuspended in 100 μL of CSM. 10 μL of nuclei in suspension were transferred onto a microscope slide, a coverslip was placed on top, and samples were imaged using the Keyence microscope BZ-X800. The images confirmed that the isolated nuclei were minimally contaminated with micronuclei or cellular debris (
Figure S8
B).
Sample processing and antibody staining of isolated nuclei for CyTOF analysis
Fixed, frozen TYK-nu nuclei were thawed at RT and transferred into cluster tubes containing 1 mL of cold CSM. The samples were washed at 600 × g for 10 min at 4°C. Next, nuclei were permeabilized by incubating in 1 mL of 100% ice-cold methanol for 20 min at 4°C, then washed twice with cold CSM. The samples were stained for 1 h at RT on a shaker with antibodies against vimentin (D21H3, CST) and intra-nuclear proteins (Histone H3 [clone D1H2, Standard BioTools] and cleaved PARP [clone F21-852, BD]). Following staining, samples were washed twice with cold CSM and incubated overnight at 4°C in 1 mL of a solution containing the
191
/
193
Ir DNA intercalator (0.1 μM) in 1.6% PFA prepared in PBS. After incubation, the nuclei were washed once with CSM and twice with CyTOF water, then resuspended in a solution containing normalization beads and introduced into the CyTOF2 instrument. Platinum was detected on the 195 or 198 channel, corresponding to its most abundant stable isotope.
For data analysis, nuclei—comprising both non-apoptotic and apoptotic populations—were initially gated using a 2D plot of
191
Ir versus
193
Ir intensities, a method routinely employed to identify single cells in CyTOF analysis (
Figure S8
C). Because iridium serves as a DNA intercalator, this gating step highly enriches nuclei. To further enhance purity, a subsequent gate was applied using an antibody against Histone H3 to exclude micronuclei and nuclear fragments with low histone H3 expression. Additional gating steps involved using
103
Rh staining to exclude dead cells and cleaved PARP staining to distinguish apoptotic from non-apoptotic nuclei. Both nuclear populations were then analyzed for platinum content and the data are presented on boxplots (
Figure 2
E).

Cell cycle distribution was measured by applying the manual gating strategy described previously.

LDA was performed using the MASS package in R. Viable single-cell data from HeLa cells were used. For each treatment condition (class), 7,000 cells were randomly sampled. Single cell data visualization and dimensionality reduction
Single-cell CyTOF data were processed and visualized using the Scanpy package in Python.

k

Clustering, partition-based graph extraction (PAGA), and diffusion pseudo-time (DPT)
Single cell data were clustered with the Leiden algorithm using the scanpy package in Python.
62
The Leiden algorithm was selected due to its improved accuracy in identifying well-connected communities. In this study, clustering was not used to define discrete cell phenotypes, but rather to group cells with similar characteristics, such as cell cycle phase, treatment, or fate, for contextual analysis within the larger dataset. The goal was to generate enough clusters to capture the structure of the cellular manifold while keeping the number low enough to enable reasonable visualization and downstream analyses. Clustering was performed separately for the TYK-nu and UWB time course experiments. For both datasets, pre-processed as described in the previous section, a nearest neighbor graph with k = 30 nearest neighbors was constructed, and Leiden clustering with resolution = 5.0 was run. Results were visualized in ggplot2. Following clustering, PAGA was used to compute the connectivity between the identified clusters with default parameters.
63
Edges with PAGA weights less than 0.1 were excluded. PAGA graphs were visualized in the R igraph package. Diffusion pseudo-time (DPT) was computed with default parameters using the scanpy package (

Non-negative matrix factorization (NMF)
NMF was computed using the consensus NMF approach with the scikit-learn package in Python.
64
To denoise the data, cells with total expression (sum over all marker expression levels) higher than the 99.5% quantile were excluded. Data were then row normalized and scaled to unit variance. Consensus NMF modules were then computed by computing 100 sets of modules using the NMF function in scikit-learn, with max_iter = 3000. K was set to 30 for KNN-deviation and only modules that fall within a distance threshold of 0.1 were kept. Resulting modules were visualized using the gplots package in R and ComplexHeatmap (
Figures 4
F and
5
H). For cell line specific NMF, eight modules were computed using the above approach for each cell line separately. Boxplots showing module activity over time were generated in ggplot2.
Prediction of treatment-response module activity
The activity of NMF DDR modules previously computed from TYK-nu cells was estimated in CIOV1, CIOV2, CIOV3, OVCAR3, and JHOS2 cell lines using the scikit-learn package in Python.

Introduction
Cytotoxic chemotherapy remains a critically important treatment for cancer patients worldwide and is effective against rapidly dividing tumor cells in which the DNA damage response (DDR) is deregulated from cell-cycle control.
1
,
2
,
3
However, durable patient outcomes are rare, even in individuals with enhanced innate sensitivity. This is due to the acquisition and selection of complex cellular traits that result in therapeutic resistance compounded further by influence from the tumor microenvironment (TME).
4
,
5
,
6
The standard of care for women with tubo-ovarian high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC) remains carboplatin-based chemotherapy either following surgery or in a neoadjuvant setting.
7
,
8
,
9
,
10
,
11
,
12
Most patients (∼60%) initially respond because of frequent impairment of DDR pathways, but almost all will develop fatal platinum-resistant recurrent disease.
13
,
14
The exact mechanisms behind clinical platinum resistance are not well understood, and, consequently, there are no effective medicines specifically designed to target carboplatin resistance.
Although multiple potential resistance mechanisms have been described, including genomic alterations, enhanced DNA repair capabilities, and increased drug transporter activity, they have shown limited clinical impact.
10
,
15
,
16
,
17
However, the importance of genetic reversion as a mechanism of resistance is strongly supported by clinical studies in patients with
BRCA1
and
BRCA2
reversion mutations. These studies have demonstrated that tumors can acquire secondary somatic mutations that restore the function of homologous recombination (HR), thereby contributing to resistance to both carboplatin and poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitors (PARPi).
18
,
19
,
20
,
21
,
22
Furthermore,
post hoc
analysis of clinical data from patients treated with first-line carboplatin with PARPi maintenance suggested rewiring of the DDR toward subsequent platinum treatment.
23
Although HGSC tumors are primarily driven by DNA structural variants, especially copy-number alterations,
24
,
25
there are very few new genomic changes in a recurrent tumor,
26
although possible effects from extrachromosomal DNA need to be further explored.
27
Additionally, methylation and gene expression integrated with other omics data reported by The Ovarian Cancer Genome Atlas have highlighted the complexity of resistance but without identifying any specific therapeutic targets.
28
Single-cell RNA sequencing studies in ovarian cancer cell line models showed a stepwise trajectory of adaptation to PARPi treatment with a progressive acquisition of resistance. These trajectories are potentiated by epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition states and maintained by diverse reprogramming of metabolic and stress phenotypes.
29
Together, these studies suggest that HGSC tumors are susceptible to a broad evolutionary space to escape carboplatin and PARPi therapies.
Although the upstream genetic, epigenetic, and transcriptomic effects are likely highly diverse, they necessarily converge on protein function within the DDR network. Critically, the DDR is regulated by protein expression levels and phosphorylation states.
30
,
31
,
32
,
33
,
34
Based on the reported heterogeneity of resistance phenotypes and possible DDR responses, we hypothesized that (1) single-cell proteomic analysis is required to identify diverse DDR protein networks indicative of sensitivity or resistance to carboplatin and (2) comparable levels of carboplatin uptake by individual cells will result in different DDRs. To address our hypotheses, we applied mass cytometry, known as CyTOF/cytometry by time-of-flight to measure the DDR in HGSC tumor cells. CyTOF is a single-cell proteomic technology that measures up to 60 parameters per cell using a panel of antibodies conjugated to heavy metal-chelating polymers.
35
,
36
,
37
We assembled a CyTOF antibody panel to simultaneously measure the DDR, cell-cycle phase, and intracellular signaling in response to carboplatin alone or in combination with a PARPi. Key to this study was the ability to relate our results to the uptake of platinum in individual cells since the atomic mass of platinum falls within the measurable mass range of CyTOF. Our study used HGSC model systems that, based on prior characterization, share key molecular and phenotypic features with primary tumors.

Unsupervised analysis of millions of single cells discovered DDR protein modules recruited by cells in specific states after treatment.

By contrast, other cells treated for 24 h mapped closely to cells treated for 96 h and were in proximity to apoptotic cells (

Non-negative matrix factorization to discover modules of co-occurring DDR proteins and their activity over time in single cells
The UMAP/PAGA analysis revealed clusters with different DDRs (
Figure 4
). To determine if specific DDR proteins influenced the positioning of cells along the PAGA trajectories, we applied non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) (
Figure 4
F). This algorithm simultaneously learns a set of co-occurring proteins within DDR protein modules and then computes the activity of each module in each cell.
64
NMF computed eight DDR protein modules, and the contribution of each protein to each module was visualized with a heatmap (
Figure 4
F). Several proteins occupied more than one module. For example, PARP1 was part of modules 2 and 8 and proliferating cell nuclear antigen (PCNA) was part of modules 2 and 4 (
Figure 4
F). To determine the activity of different modules over duration of treatment, modules were overlaid on the UMAP (
Figure 4
G). Rather than being uniformly distributed, the activity of most modules showed a tendency to localize within specific regions of the DDR cellular landscape over the time course (
Figure 4
G). Specifically, module 1 localized to apoptotic cells, module 4 to untreated cells with endogenous DDR, module 7 to mitotic cells, and module 6 to pre-apoptotic cells. However, when module activity was visualized on the PAGA graph, cells frequently exhibited overlapping activation of multiple modules, indicating that individual DDR states are composed of contributions from several distinct modules (
Figure S11
).
To further characterize module activity shown in the UMAP overlays, we generated box plots (
Figure 4
H). The plots showed that module activity in individual cells changed over time but at different rates. Modules 2 and 8 were active at early times and detected in both endogenous and treatment-induced DDRs, while module 4 was most active in untreated cells. Module 3 peaked early after treatment and included MRE11 and NBS1 consistent with their role as early sensors of DNA damage. Module 6 demonstrated the greatest change over time, bridging pre-apoptotic and apoptotic cell states and largely driven by carboplatin (
Figures 4
G and 4H). Module 6 comprised pH2AX, pATM, pCHK1, pp53, and pRPA, proteins with critical roles in the DDR that function in damage sensing, signaling, and checkpoint activation following double-strand breaks.
65
The continuous increase in module 6 activity over time after carboplatin exposure suggested it could be a pharmacodynamic marker of sensitivity to carboplatin-induced DNA damage. The key finding from the UMAP/PAGA/NMF analysis was that, although most non-apoptotic cells mapped as a continuum on the UMAP, they were functionally distinguishable by way of eight distinct DDR protein modules.

To determine changes in the DDR during carboplatin exposure in UWB cells, we discovered eight DDR modules using NMF. The relative contribution of each protein within a module was depicted with a heatmap (

Discussion
Our study was predicated on the hypothesis that in response to carboplatin ovarian tumor cells selectively activate specific DDR protein sub-networks or modules through changes in phosphorylation and abundance. Activating the entire DDR network would be metabolically inefficient. We capitalized on the single-cell attributes of CyTOF to measure the carboplatin-mediated DDR. To understand why cells with comparable levels of intranuclear carboplatin underwent divergent fates, we analyzed CyTOF datasets with an unsupervised approach using UMAP embedding, PAGA, and NMF (
Figure 3
). We observed a continuum of cells exhibiting subtle to large differences in their DDR states that aligns with a recent study showing that ovarian tumor cells transition through a series of transcriptomic states as they progress toward resistance to a PARPi
29
(
Figures 4
and
5
). The eight NMF DDR protein modules identified in TYK-nu and UWB cells provided deeper mechanistic insight into these DDR states. For the most part, simultaneous multimodule activity (and not reliance on a single module) was shared by both sensitive and resistant cell populations enabling a dynamic and integrated DDR response but with different cellular fates. However, the activity of a single unique module containing Ki67 and pAurora reflected a DDR state specific to mitosis.
70
,
71
While reversion mutants of
BRCA1
and
BRCA2
confer resistance by restoring HR, stable reintroduction of
BRCA1
into UWB-
BRCA1
-null cells did not change module activity or restore carboplatin sensitivity, suggesting that these cells had acquired BRCA1-independent mechanisms of carboplatin resistance.
18
,
21
For TYK-nu and UWB cells, early activity of modules containing the transcription factors phosphorylated nuclear factor kappa B (pNFκB), Myc, and β-catenin (module 3 in TYK-nu and module 2 in UWB) aligned with their known roles in chemoresistance, stemness, and survival.
72
,
73
,
74
The coordinated activation of pRPA, pATM, pH2AX, and pCHK1 or pCHK2 (module 6 in TYK-nu and module 8 in UWB) indicated a canonical DDR to carboplatin: pH2AX and pATM mark double-strand breaks, pRPA indicates replication stress, and pCHK1 or pCHK2 signal cell-cycle arrest.
65
,
75
In sensitive cells, this intact damage-sensing network may become overwhelmed with consequent failed DNA repair and commitment to apoptosis. Consistent with our findings, a recent study showed that HR-proficient HGSCs with high levels of pRPA32(T21) had superior survival outcomes.
76
In contrast, resistant cells may evade activity of the canonical DDR through impaired sensing of DNA damage, enhanced repair, or checkpoint bypass. In support of this, UWB cells showed reduced activity of module 8 at later time points (24–72 h) and greater reliance on the more complex module 5, consistent with a resistance-maintaining response and their previously reported transcriptomic complexity (
Figures 5
I and 5J).
28
,
29
,
41
Of note, the activity of module 5 was seen in some clusters of pre- and apoptotic cells suggesting that in some cases cells fail to maintain a resistant state.
In the CIOV models, module 6 consistently emerged as the most robust indicator of carboplatin sensitivity with a clear gradient of activity: greatest in carboplatin-sensitive CIOV1, lowest in innate-resistant CIOV2, and intermediate in acquired-resistant CIOV3, underscoring its potential as a functional biomarker, independent of genetic background. Module 6 activity increased further with carboplatin plus rucaparib treatment, particularly in CIOV1, suggesting that this module may capture additive or synergistic DDRs. By contrast, carboplatin plus paclitaxel induced lower module 6 activity, perhaps because paclitaxel targets microtubules and cell division rather than a direct effect on the DDR network.
The presence of EMT and mesenchymal cell phenotypes in CIOV2 and CIOV3 is consistent with their resistance characteristics.
77
However, the more epithelial phenotypes for cells in G1 suggest a mechanism whereby E-cadherin, through its cell-adhesive function with β-catenin, may regulate levels of transcriptionally active β-catenin and its target genes associated with proliferation such as
MYC
and
CCND1
.
78
In contrast, the shift toward a more mesenchymal phenotype during S-phase and G2 may enable cells to over-ride cell-cycle checkpoint arrest and adapt to carboplatin-mediated DNA damage.
77
This study is limited by the inherent complexity of DDR. Our CyTOF panel did not provide full coverage of the DDR, thus potentially missing additional DDR modules. Nevertheless, it successfully measured 36 phosphorylation states and protein levels with established roles in the DDR, cell-cycle regulation, and signaling.
65
,
75
,
79
Although this study did not include primary tumor samples or account for immune and stromal components within the TME, focusing on tumor cell autonomous mechanisms is a critical first step in unraveling DDR complexity linked to carboplatin resistance.
Many of a tumor’s adaptive responses to therapy are targetable.
33
However, inter-patient differences in innate sensitivity to carboplatin, and the evolution of acquired resistance, make it challenging to determine which adaptive pathways to target and at what point during a patient’s treatment journey. Within this context, module 6 activity emerged as a signature strongly associated with carboplatin sensitivity. We propose that monitoring module 6 activity in drug or CRISPR screens using CIOV models with clinically relevant resistant states may identify effective therapeutic combinations or gene targets that could pre-empt or reverse carboplatin-resistant cell states. Furthermore, our cell-suspension CyTOF assay can be readily adapted for spatial analyses allowing for broader characterization of resistance modules in preclinical and clinical settings. This will guide the refinement of antibody panels for capturing both DDR and immune responses in clinical trial samples. Importantly, single-cell multiplex proteomic technologies are ideally suited to address the challenges of tumor cell heterogeneity. Our approach is generalizable to study drug resistance in other malignancies.
Limitations of the study
We were not able to provide complete coverage of the carboplatin-mediated DDR owing to (1) a maximum number of 45 antibodies that can be simultaneously studied using available stable metal isotopes for CyTOF and (2) the unavailability of reliable antibodies against BRCA1 and BRCA2. Our study was designed to elucidate tumor cell-intrinsic DDR mechanisms, and we did not evaluate how cell-extrinsic factors, from immune and stromal cells in the TME, may modulate the DDR. Future experiments will test the activity of module 6 in clinically annotated samples from primary or interval debulking to evaluate its potential as a predictive marker for response to platinum-based chemotherapy. Additionally, we will evaluate the effects of immune and stromal cells on the activity of module 6 by applying spatial multiplex proteomics with expanded antibody panels to these clinical samples.

Experimental model and subject details
Clinical data and tissue samples from patients were collected on the prospective Cambridge Translational Cancer Research Ovarian Study 04 (CTCR-OV04) with Research Ethics Committee approval 08/H0306/61. Patients provided written, informed consent for participation in this study and for the use of their donated tissue for the laboratory studies carried out in this work. Out of 93 samples three spontaneously immortalized continuous HGSOC cell lines were generated, named CIOV1, CIOV2, and CIOV3, and used as part of this study.

Cell lines
HeLa and OVCAR3 (American Type Culture Collection (ATCC)) and TYK-nu (National Institute of Biomedical Innovation, Japanese Collection of Research Bioresources Cell Bank (JCRB)) cell lines were cultured in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) (Gibco), McCoy’s 5A modified medium (Gibco) and Eagle’s minimal essential medium (EMEM) (ATCC) respectively supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS) (Hyclone), 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin (Gibco) and 2 mM L-glutamine (Gibco). CIOV1, CIOV2 and CIOV3 cell lines (Brenton Lab, University of Cambridge, UK) were cultured in DMEM/F-12 medium (Gibco) with 10% FBS and 1% penicillin/streptomycin. Research design summary
To investigate tumor cell-intrinsic DDR mechanisms underlying carboplatin resistance and sensitivity, we performed single-cell mass cytometry (CyTOF) profiling across a panel of HGSC cell lines, that phenocopy human tumors, comprised of TYK-nu, the highly resistant UWB1.289 BRCA1-and UWB1.289 BRCA1+ isogenic pair, JHOS2, OVCAR3, and patient-derived models (CIOV1, CIOV2 and CIOV3). The UWB1.289 BRCA1-deficient cell line was derived from an HGSC tumor that recurred following primary debulking surgery and multiple lines of chemotherapy, including carboplatin/paclitaxel, paclitaxel alone, topotecan, and gemcitabine combined with doxorubicin. It harbors a clinically deleterious allele of
BRCA1
with loss of heterozygosity at the
BRCA1
locus rendering it null for BRCA1 protein function. The UWB1.289+BRCA1 cell line has partial restoration of BRCA1 function from stable expression of a
BRCA1
cDNA construct.
41
Cells were treated with carboplatin alone or in combination with other agents and sampled over time up to 96 h to capture dynamic DDR signaling. The CyTOF antibody panel quantified total and phosphorylated DDR proteins at single-cell resolution. Data were analyzed using unsupervised clustering and dimensionality reduction techniques to identify DDR modules and signaling trajectories across models with varying carboplatin sensitivity (
Figure 3
).

Protocol for isolating nuclei
TYK-nu cells (4–5 × 10
6
) were harvested at 24 h, 48 h, 72 h, and 96 h following carboplatin treatment. Two untreated controls were harvested at 24 h and 96 h. Each sample was divided in half for processing by flow cytometry, and CyTOF analysis. For nuclear isolation, cell pellets were resuspended in 300 μL of cold lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 10 mM NaCl, 3 mM MgCl
2

The nuclei suspension was then filtered through a 35 μm cell strainer to remove debris and nuclear aggregates. Nuclei were then fixed in 1 mL of 1.6% PFA in PBS for 10 min at RT, washed twice with cold CSM, resuspended in 150–200 μL of CSM, snap-frozen on dry ice, and stored at −80°C until flow cytometry or CyTOF analysis. Nuclear purity was validated by three independent methods.
Processing isolated nuclei for flow cytometry
Fixed frozen TYK-nu cells or nuclei were thawed at RT and transferred to FACS tubes containing 1 mL of ice-cold CSM. Samples were centrifuged at 500 × g for 10 min at 4°C. Cells and nuclei were then stained with DAPI (500 μL, 0.1 μg/mL in PBS) for 10 min at RT to assess viability and nuclear content. Following staining, 1.5 mL of cold CSM was added, and samples were centrifuged again (500 × g, 10 min, 4°C). After two additional washes with ice-cold CSM, cells and nuclei were resuspended in cold CSM at a concentration of 1–2 × 10
6
cells/mL and 0.5–1 × 10
6
nuclei/mL, for introduction into the FACS LSRII. We used forward scatter (FSC) and side scatter (SSC) parameters to distinguish nuclei from whole cells (
Figure S8
A).
Processing isolated nuclei for immunofluorescence microscopy
Fixed frozen TYK-nu nuclei were thawed at RT, transferred to FACS tubes containing 1 mL of cold CSM and washed (500 × g, 10 min, 4°C). Samples were permeabilized in 100% ice-cold methanol (1 mL) for 20 min at 4°C, washed twice with cold CSM and stained with vimentin-A647 antibody (5 μL in 100 μL of reaction) (clone D21H3 from CST) for 30 min on ice. After the addition of 2 mL CSM, samples were washed twice with CSM followed by staining with DAPI (blue fluorescence channel) (1 μg/mL in CSM, 500 μL) for 10 min at room temperature. After two washes with CSM, nuclei were resuspended in 100 μL of CSM. 10 μL of nuclei in suspension were transferred onto a microscope slide, a coverslip was placed on top, and samples were imaged using the Keyence microscope BZ-X800. The images confirmed that the isolated nuclei were minimally contaminated with micronuclei or cellular debris (
Figure S8
B).
Sample processing and antibody staining of isolated nuclei for CyTOF analysis
Fixed, frozen TYK-nu nuclei were thawed at RT and transferred into cluster tubes containing 1 mL of cold CSM. The samples were washed at 600 × g for 10 min at 4°C. Next, nuclei were permeabilized by incubating in 1 mL of 100% ice-cold methanol for 20 min at 4°C, then washed twice with cold CSM. The samples were stained for 1 h at RT on a shaker with antibodies against vimentin (D21H3, CST) and intra-nuclear proteins (Histone H3 [clone D1H2, Standard BioTools] and cleaved PARP [clone F21-852, BD]). Following staining, samples were washed twice with cold CSM and incubated overnight at 4°C in 1 mL of a solution containing the
191
/
193
Ir DNA intercalator (0.1 μM) in 1.6% PFA prepared in PBS. After incubation, the nuclei were washed once with CSM and twice with CyTOF water, then resuspended in a solution containing normalization beads and introduced into the CyTOF2 instrument. Platinum was detected on the 195 or 198 channel, corresponding to its most abundant stable isotope.
For data analysis, nuclei—comprising both non-apoptotic and apoptotic populations—were initially gated using a 2D plot of

Clustering, partition-based graph extraction (PAGA), and diffusion pseudo-time (DPT)
Single cell data were clustered with the Leiden algorithm using the scanpy package in Python.
62
The Leiden algorithm was selected due to its improved accuracy in identifying well-connected communities. In this study, clustering was not used to define discrete cell phenotypes, but rather to group cells with similar characteristics, such as cell cycle phase, treatment, or fate, for contextual analysis within the larger dataset. The goal was to generate enough clusters to capture the structure of the cellular manifold while keeping the number low enough to enable reasonable visualization and downstream analyses. Clustering was performed separately for the TYK-nu and UWB time course experiments. For both datasets, pre-processed as described in the previous section, a nearest neighbor graph with k = 30 nearest neighbors was constructed, and Leiden clustering with resolution = 5.0 was run. Results were visualized in ggplot2. Following clustering, PAGA was used to compute the connectivity between the identified clusters with default parameters.
63
Edges with PAGA weights less than 0.1 were excluded. PAGA graphs were visualized in the R igraph package. Diffusion pseudo-time (DPT) was computed with default parameters using the scanpy package (

NMF was computed using the consensus NMF approach with the scikit-learn package in Python.
